You are an independent classifier in a blinded experiment about a book of
biblical symbolism. The consensus responses below were produced without access
to the book. Compare them with the book's entry.

TERM
Belief, to believe

BLIND CONSENSUS RESPONSES
RESPONSE A
{
  "primary_meaning": "In mainstream Christian teaching, 'belief' or 'to believe' (Greek pisteuō, Hebrew aman) is understood not as mere intellectual assent to facts but as personal trust in, reliance upon, and committed entrusting of oneself to God and to Jesus Christ, resulting in salvation and eternal life. It is the receptive act by which a person appropriates God's grace — trusting Christ's person and work rather than one's own merit. Classic theology unpacks it as three elements: notitia (knowledge of the content), assensus (assent that it is true), and fiducia (personal trust), with fiducia regarded as the decisive, saving element.",

    "John 3:16",

    "John 6:29",

    "Mark 1:15",
    "Galatians 2:16"
  ],

      "meaning": "Belief as intellectual assent alone (accepting propositions as true). Christian tradition generally treats this as insufficient by itself, citing James 2:19 ('even the demons believe—and shudder'), but some strands (e.g., certain 'free grace' teachers and popular usage) effectively reduce believing to assent to gospel facts.",

        "1 John 5:1"
      ],

    },

      "meaning": "Belief as faithfulness, allegiance, or covenant loyalty — pistis rendered as ongoing fidelity and embodied allegiance to Jesus as King, not a one-time inward act. Associated with the Hebrew sense of 'emunah and with recent scholarship (e.g., Matthew Bates, 'Salvation by Allegiance Alone') and with New Perspective on Paul discussions.",

        "Habakkuk 2:4",

Emphasized in Catholic, Orthodox, and Arminian/Wesleyan traditions and in James; Protestants typically frame this as 'faith alone, but not a faith that is alone.'",

        "James 2:14-26",

      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Belief as itself a divine gift and effect of grace or election, not a purely human act — the Reformed/Augustinian emphasis that God grants faith.",

      ],

    {
      "meaning": "Belief as mystical union or abiding participation in Christ — Johannine emphasis where believing means coming to, feeding on, and abiding in Christ, stressed in sacramental and contemplative traditions.",

        "John 6:35, 6:47-58",
        "John 15:1-11",
        "Galatians 2:20"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    }
  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": true,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "There is a broad, recognizable consensus across Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant traditions that biblical 'believing' means saving trust/entrustment in God and in Christ, exceeding bare mental assent. The live disputes are secondary and concern emphasis: whether faith is best glossed as trust, allegiance/faithfulness, or gift; how faith relates to works (the James–Paul discussion); and whether faith is a one-time act or persevering disposition. These are debates within a settled core rather than competing symbolic meanings. The term is more a theological concept than a 'symbol' in the typological sense; interpreters treat it literally-theologically rather than allegorically."

  "notes": "There is broad Christian consensus that “belief” centrally involves faith or trust, particularly trust in God and Christ. There is no single settled symbolic interpretation because the biblical words translated “believe” normally function as direct theological and relational language rather than as a conventional symbol. Disagreement concerns whether particular occurrences emphasize factual assent, personal trust, loyalty, obedience, divine enablement, or some combination of these."

The term is largely functional/theological rather than a free-floating symbol like water or light."

BOOK ENTRY
Receiving God's testimony as true and governing, then acting upon it. Mere assent can acknowledge a fact; persistent refusal to obey exposes unbelief.

BOOK'S COMMON-VIEW NOTE, IF PRESENT
Commonly taught: personal trust in Christ, not mere assent — the instrument that receives salvation.

SCRIPTURE REFERENCES PRINTED WITH THE ENTRY
(Mark 1:27; John 3:36; 12:42-43; Rom 10:16; Heb 3:18-19; Jas 2:19-22) · see Love, Knowing, Faith & Belief, ch. 6

AVAILABLE KJV EXCERPTS
Mark 1:27 — And they were all amazed, insomuch that they questioned among themselves, saying, What thing is this? what new doctrine is this? for with authority commandeth he even the unclean spirits, and they do obey him.
John 3:36 — He that believeth on the Son hath everlasting life: and he that believeth not the Son shall not see life; but the wrath of God abideth on him.
John 12:42 — Nevertheless among the chief rulers also many believed on him; but because of the Pharisees they did not confess him, lest they should be put out of the synagogue:
John 12:43 — For they loved the praise of men more than the praise of God.
Romans 10:16 — But they have not all obeyed the gospel. For Esaias saith, Lord, who hath believed our report?
Hebrews 3:18 — And to whom sware he that they should not enter into his rest, but to them that believed not?
Hebrews 3:19 — So we see that they could not enter in because of unbelief.
James 2:19 — Thou believest that there is one God; thou doest well: the devils also believe, and tremble.
James 2:20 — But wilt thou know, O vain man, that faith without works is dead?
James 2:21 — Was not Abraham our father justified by works, when he had offered Isaac his son upon the altar?
James 2:22 — Seest thou how faith wrought with his works, and by works was faith made perfect?

CLASSIFY THE RELATIONSHIP

First reduce both readings to their minimum core identifications. Do not let
extra detail create an artificial disagreement.

- MATCH: the core identifications are equivalent. Differences are merely
  wording or immaterial detail.
- REFINED: the book preserves the consensus's general referent or category but
  materially changes its extension, boundary, conditions, or precision. A
  narrowing may reject some cases the broader consensus admits; a broadening
  may admit cases it excludes. This is real disagreement at the boundary, but
  not replacement of the central referent.
- DIVERGENT: the cores materially contradict. Both claims cannot be true of the
  same referent in the same context and sense; accepting the book requires
  rejecting or replacing the consensus identification. A source and its
  product remain different referents when the book explicitly denies their
  identity, even if they are causally related.
- NOVEL: no recognizable consensus or listed alternative covers the book's
  core identification. Novelty is absence from consensus, not contradiction.

Use `core_relation` to expose the relationship at the center and
`extension_relation` to expose disagreement over the cases covered. A REFINED
verdict must state what cases the book adds, excludes, or reclassifies. A
DIVERGENT verdict must identify a replaced referent or material contradiction,
not merely a narrower boundary.

Treat the two axes independently. A core-divergent reading may still retain
some cases covered by the consensus while rejecting its central identification;
therefore DIVERGENT does not require disjoint extensions. Conversely, a
narrowed extension is REFINED only when the consensus's central referent or
category remains intact.

Also judge whether the citations printed with the glossary entry alone provide
strong, partial, or insufficient support. Do not yet decide whether a divergent
full chapter is persuasive; that is a separate stage.
